newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian minister suspended in sauna video row.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister suspended in sauna video row.

text.p: Russia's justice minister, caught up in a scandal over a video film showing naked sauna scenes, will be removed from office temporarily pending an inquiry, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Sunday.
Valentin Kovalyov, who is also a member of Russia's top-level Security Council, asked President Boris Yeltsin on Saturday to suspend him while he cleared his name.
His request was most unusual and came after the monthly newspaper Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret) published grainy snaps taken from the video. It alleged they showed him in a sauna with women.

"We will suspend him temporarily from his duties," Chernomyrdin told reporters after laying a wreath at Moscow's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier -- Sunday was the anniversary of Nazi Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941.
"But things have to be investigated. I would prefer not to make any decisions based just on the publication," he added.
Kovalyov's lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, said the minister was the victim of a smear campaign and warned the mass media about rushing to premature conclusions without adequate information.

"I am absolutely sure and convinced that the campaign now being waged against the minister is aimed, in the first place, at discrediting his name and, secondly, his office," Kucherena told NTV commercial television.
"Today we do not know where this information originated and until an investigation has been conducted and until the law has had its final say there is no point talking about it," he said.
Chernomyrdin said the ball was now in Kovalyov's court.

"Kovalyov denies everything," said Chernomyrdin, who recalled the 53-year-old former law professor from a foreign trip on Friday when the story broke. "He is a lawyer. He knows how to defend himself. Let him prove it is not true."
He added: "If it is true, it is very sad for all of us, just sad. Such behaviour is not becoming to a government minister, or indeed any person. We will sort it out."
In a country long known for official secrecy, few, if any, Russian ministers have had to resign because of scandals. In the Soviet era, newspapers almost never put the spotlight on serving ministers.
Moscow's powerful mayor, Yuri Luzhkov, told reporters Kovalyov should quit. He described the allegations as "inadmissible for a person in such an important job".

Russian television stations have broadcast brief but somewhat indistinct excerpts from the black-and-white video, clearly shot using a hidden camera. Top Secret said the video was shot at a gangland nightclub sauna in September 1995. Kovalyov became justice minister in January of that year.

Kovalyov said in a statement on Saturday he had nothing to be ashamed of and was seeking to be suspended to defend his good name and the government's dignity. He hinted he would take legal action against the newspaper.
"This request is by no means a recognition of the validity of the report but is out of consideration for the government's prestige," he said. "This is my top priority."
Kovalyov said it was well known that computers could be used to manipulate images and place a person "in any situation".
"This is not technically difficult," he said.

Yeltsin was in the United States at a world summit and has not reacted to the story. A government spokesman said on Saturday he was aware of it but was unlikely to respond formally to Kovalyov's request until Monday.
Chernomyrdin has the authority to suspend ministers but the request was addressed to Yeltsin. Only the president can sack ministers.
